newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower on strong economic data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower on strong economic data.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended sharply lower on Thursday after two strong economic reports and comments by Federal Reserve officials strengthened the view that the Fed would raise interest rates, perhaps soon.

The government's report that retail sales rose a stronger than expected 0.8 percent in February after a revised 1.5 percent jump in January unnerved the market early in the session. The government also reported that new claims for unemployment insurance totaled just 307,000 in the latest week, down from a revised 312,000 a week earlier.
The four-week moving average for new jobless claims now stands at 310,250. Economists said the subdued level of claims suggested the March employment picture would be strong.

After weakening in the morning, bond prices fell again in conjunction with public comments of two Fed officials. Fed Vice Chairman Alice Rivlin said the Fed needs to be especially vigilant against the threat of faster inflation. And Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Michael Moskow said the U.S. central bank must have a preemptive policy to foil inflationary pressures that might threaten the economy's long-term growth.
These comments gave another bout of jitters to investors who worry the Fed will raise interest rates as soon as its March 25 policy meeting and prompted further selling.

In the Chicago futures market, the June T-bond contract broke below support at 108-23/32, the low for the contract set on Friday, March 7, after the February employment report was released. At that juncture, the benchmark 30-year bond yield extended its loss to just over a full point.
The market's inclination toward selling was curbed a bit, however, by awareness of Friday's Producer Price Index (PPI) report for February, strategists said.
While the Fed has a batch of data in hand to support the argument that the economy is growing quite strongly, the bin of evidence to show inflation picking up is nearly empty.
The February PPI, due on Friday, is expected to be a very friendly piece of data for the inflation-wary credit markets.
Economists polled by Reuters forecast, on average, that the PPI slipped 0.1 percent in February after a 0.3 percent decline in January.
The so-called core PPI, the index minus its more volatile food and energy items, is forecast to be up 0.1 percent, after registering no change in January.

Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that retail sales rose 0.6 percent in February and 0.7 percent when auto sales were excluded. In January, sales rose 0.6 percent and just 0.4 percent when auto sales were deleted.
"The (imminent) PPI report prevented some people from blowing out of positions," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.

But Stiles said that with the market so focused on the Fed's apparent inclination to move pre-emptively against inflation, data reflecting strong demand in the economy would influence the market more than benign inflation numbers.
The benchmark 30-year bond ended at 95-26/32, down 30/32, its yield at 6.96 percent, the highest in nearly six months.

At the short end of the maturity range, three-month bill rates rose four basis points to 5.10 percent. Six-month bill rates rose two basis points to 5.20 percent and year bill rates rose four basis points to 5.42 percent.
Two-year notes slipped 3/32 at 99-15/32, yielding 6.16 percent. Five-year notes were down 12/32 to 98-26/32, yielding 6.53 percent. Ten-year notes fell 21/32 to 96-24/32, yielding 6.70 percent.
